subject: Want to model effect of group size on (g0)

messages.author: 732b7d3e3bc82091
messages.subject: Want to model effect of group size on (g0)
parts:
Dear Sir,
I am Keshab from Wildlife Institute of India, working on Asiatic lion.
Sir, lion being social in nature, their detection probability could highly dependent on the size of their groups. Which I wanted to model in secr analysis. I have individual id, group id and size of the groups. If I want to model (g0) on size of the groups, how could I proceed for that? Could you kindly give your valuable suggestions in this regards..?

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Want to model effect of group size on (g0)
parts:
Hello Keshab

This is a question for which I don't know a simple answer. The main SECR models assume detections occur independently, so there is a fundamental difficulty with social animals that are sighted as a group. Distance methods switch to counting whole groups and adjusting for average group size. It is not usually possible to do this with passive detections in SECR. Although it may be technically possible if you are visually detecting groups, probably you have too few groups for this to be a sensible solution. Perhaps SECR is just not an appropriate method. I can imagine a complex hierarchical model that allowed for grouping, but I can't help any further on that.

You could go through the motions of fitting an SECR model in secr ignoring the independence question. In that case group size - if it is constant over time - is like other individual covariates: include it as an extra column in your capture file, name it with the covnames argument of read.capthist, and use the name in a formula for g0 or sigma when fitting a conditional likelihood model 
CH <- read.capthist(..., covnames = 'groupsize')
fit <- secr.fit(CH, CL = TRUE, model = list(g0~groupsize))
derived(fit)
(This will take a long time to fit, especially if there are many different group sizes).

If group size varies (I assume it does) then we don't have an answer at present, but you could possibly use an average for each individual. I emphasise that I don't know of canned solutions that are proven to work for social animals, but others are working in this area.

Murray
